533.title: Living ashtpadi 24
533.hook: the psalm ends where it began: peace in remembering
533.howItsDone: Sukhmani Sahib opens with simran bringing peace and closes on the same Name, and Sikhs recite it daily or weekly, alone or together, returning to that circle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amrit, and your line: the name is peace. Did you set down one load on a single breath? Today we live the last ashtpadi, and find that Sukhmani has been walking in a circle all along. Day five hundred thirty-three.

A round is a song that chases itself. One voice starts, a second joins a line later, then a third, and the tune keeps circling back to its own beginning. Children learn them at camp around a fire. The fun is that there's no real ending: when you reach the last line, you're already back at the first. Sukhmani is long: twenty-four ashtpadis. But when you reach the last one, you find you've come back around. It ends where it began.
screen: `A SONG THAT CHASES ITSELF.` → `NO REAL ENDING.` → `BACK WHERE IT BEGAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the twenty-fourth ashtpadi in brief. Its salok rings pooraa four times: the perfect Lord, perfect Name, perfect One found and praised. Its first stanza calls us to the perfect Guru's teaching and to remember God with every breath, so the mind's anxiety lifts. And over it all hangs Sukhmani's center line: the jewel of peace is the ambrosial Name. Now go back to the very first stanza of Sukhmani, all the way at the start. It opens with a run of one word: simrau simar simar sukh paavau. In paraphrase: I remember, remembering, remembering, I find peace, and the troubles of the body are erased. Simran: remembering, keeping God in mind. And sukh: peace. That's the first line. Twenty-four ashtpadis later, the bani closes on the same two things: the Name, remembered, and the peace it brings. It ends where it began. Why does that matter for daily life? Because a circle tells you something a straight line doesn't. A straight line says: finish this, and you're done. A circle says: this is a path you walk again. Sukhmani isn't read once and filed away. Some Sikhs recite it daily, some weekly, and some gather to recite it together. Each time, the first line and the last line meet. Living ashtpadi 24 isn't reaching a finish. It's coming back around to remembering, and finding the peace was waiting there the whole time.
screen: `THE LAST ASHTPADI: PERFECT, BREATH BY BREATH.` · `SIMRAU SIMAR SIMAR: THE FIRST LINE.` · `THE SAME TWO THINGS AT THE END.` · `A CIRCLE YOU WALK AGAIN.` · then, large: `PEACE IN REMEMBERING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember, and rest. Sit and let the breath settle. For the first minute, remember, gently: someone who loves you, a time you felt held, a moment of beauty. If you pray, remember God, and let Waheguru come with the breath, like the first line of Sukhmani: remembering, remembering. For the second minute, stop remembering and just rest in whatever peace the remembering left behind. The bell holds the time.
Simran, remembering God: Sukhmani opens with simran bringing sukh, remembering bringing peace, and closes on the same Name and the same peace.
Your line: peace in remembering. Today, at the start and at the end of your day, take three breaths of remembering, so the day comes full circle. Day five hundred thirty-three.

534.title: Sukhmani whole
534.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan's twenty-four ashtpadis in raag Gauri, in a single sitting, daily or weekly, and groups gather in homes and gurdwaras to recite it together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, simran, and your line: peace in remembering. Did your day come full circle? For about a hundred days we've walked Sukhmani one piece at a time. Today we step back and see it whole. Day five hundred thirty-four.

There's a difference between studying a mosaic tile by tile and stepping back to see the picture. Up close, each tile is a small square of color: blue, gold, a chip of red. You can learn a lot about tiles that way. But step back across the room, and suddenly there's a face, a tree, a whole scene. The tiles didn't change. You just saw them together. We've been looking at Sukhmani tile by tile since day four hundred thirty-six. Today, the whole picture.
screen: `A MOSAIC, TILE BY TILE.` → `STEP BACK: A WHOLE PICTURE.` → `SUKHMANI WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Sukhmani Sahib was written by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, who also compiled the Adi Granth, the scripture that became the Guru Granth Sahib. Tradition places its writing at Ramsar, a pool in Amritsar. It sits in raag Gauri, and it's long: twenty-four ashtpadis. Ashtpadi means eight steps, and each one has a salok and then eight stanzas. Seen whole, the picture has a shape. It opens with remembering: simrau simar simar sukh paavau, remembering, I find peace. Early on, it praises simran and the company of the holy, and names the qualities of the God-conscious person. In the middle, it turns honest about us: pride, slander, cleverness, leaning on mortals, wealth that stays behind. Then it lifts toward refuge: the wanderer at the door, the beggar asking for mercy. Toward the end it opens out to the very largest things: the stillness before creation, the Lord of all beings, the cleared eyes that see God within and without. And it closes on the perfect One and the peace of the Name, back where it began. So it's not a list. It's a journey: from remembering, through an honest look at ourselves, to refuge, to wonder, to peace. Some Sikhs recite it in one sitting, daily or weekly, and families and sangats gather in homes and gurdwaras to recite it together, in hard times or at a family's milestones. Read whole, it takes time. That's part of the gift: a long stretch where nothing is asked of you but to listen.
screen: `GURU ARJAN, RAAG GAURI.` · `TWENTY-FOUR STEPS OF EIGHT.` · `REMEMBERING, HONESTY, REFUGE, WONDER, PEACE.` · `RECITED WHOLE, ALONE OR TOGETHER.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE JEWEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read it whole, once. Not in these two minutes, but plan it now. Sit quietly and choose a time this week when you'll have an hour or so: a weekend morning, a quiet evening. Picture yourself there, with the text in Gurmukhi or in a translation, or with a recording playing. Then, for the rest of the sit, simply rest and let the shape of the journey pass through your mind: remembering, honesty, refuge, wonder, peace. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Sukhmani whole. Guru Arjan's twenty-four ashtpadis, read in one sitting, make a journey from remembering, through honesty and refuge, to wonder and peace.
Your line: the whole jewel. Today, put the time you chose into your calendar, with a reminder, so the hour actually happens. Day five hundred thirty-four.

535.title: Sukhmani close
535.hook: a psalm for peace in any week
535.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Sukhmani Sahib in every kind of week, in hard times, at milestones and on ordinary days, and many keep a favorite stanza by heart to return to.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sukhmani whole, and your line: the whole jewel. Is the hour in your calendar? Today is the last day of our hundred days with Sukhmani. Tomorrow a new bani begins. Day five hundred thirty-five.

Some people keep one thing from a long trip. Not the whole suitcase of souvenirs; one thing. A smooth stone from a beach, a ticket stub, a recipe written on a napkin. Years later, holding it, the whole trip comes back: the light, the smells, who you were then. One small thing carries the rest. We've spent a hundred days walking through Sukhmani, from remembering to peace. Today, at the close, the question is simple. What will you keep?
screen: `ONE STONE FROM A LONG TRIP.` → `ONE THING CARRIES THE REST.` → `WHAT WILL YOU KEEP?`

segments.voice: Sukhmani has been called a psalm of peace, and Sikhs turn to it in every kind of week. It's recited in a hospital waiting room, before an exam, at a new baby's welcome, on the anniversary of a death, and on ordinary Tuesdays when nothing in particular is wrong. That range is the point. Its peace isn't only for good weeks or only for bad ones. Look back at what we walked. Simran: remembering, and finding peace. The God-conscious person, humble as the earth. Honest pages on pride and slander and clever schemes. Wealth that stays behind, and kindness that travels. A wanderer at the door, a beggar asking for mercy. The stillness before creation, the Lord of every living thing, the eye-ointment of wisdom, the perfect One. And at the center, the line the whole bani grows from: the jewel of peace is the ambrosial Name. Nobody holds all of that at once. That's why today's practice is to keep one ashtpadi. Many Sikhs have a favorite stanza they know by heart and return to when they need it. It's like the stone from the beach: one piece that brings the whole back. Tomorrow we move to a new bani, Asa di Var, the ballad sung at dawn in gurdwaras, by Guru Nanak, with saloks by Guru Nanak and Guru Angad. It's a very different sound: bolder, sharper, written to a folk tune. But Sukhmani doesn't end because we've moved on. It's a circle. Whatever you keep from it today, you can return to in any week.
screen: `A PSALM FOR EVERY KIND OF WEEK.` · `WHAT WE WALKED, FROM SIMRAN TO PEACE.` · `KEEP ONE PIECE, LIKE A STONE.` · `NEXT: THE BALLAD AT DAWN.` · then, large: `PEACE, KEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one ashtpadi. Sit quietly and let the last hundred days drift past. Which picture stayed? The beggar at the door, the stillness before creation, the eye-ointment, the earth that bears everything, the kindness that travels? Don't choose by thinking. Notice which one your mind keeps returning to. Let that be yours. Hold it gently for the rest of the sit, like a stone in your palm. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru with it. The bell holds the time.
Sukh, peace or ease: a psalm of peace for any week, we close our hundred days by keeping one piece of it, to bring the whole back when needed.
Your line: peace, kept. Today, write down the ashtpadi or picture you chose, and put it somewhere you'll see it next week. Day five hundred thirty-five.

536.title: The ballad at dawn
536.hook: a var is a heroic ballad; Guru Nanak's in Asa is sung before sunrise in gurdwaras
536.tomorrow: To the tune of a king's ballad
536.howItsDone: In many gurdwaras ragis sing Asa di Var in the early morning, often before sunrise, weaving in the chhants of Guru Ram Das; at the Darbar Sahib it is part of the morning kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sukh, and your line: peace, kept. Did you write down the piece you chose? Sukhmani was a long, quiet psalm. Today a new bani begins, and it has a very different sound. Day five hundred thirty-six.

At a Sikh festival, you might hear dhadis: singers with a small hourglass drum called a dhadd and a bowed sarangi, standing and singing at full voice about battles and heroes, brave deaths and great deeds. The crowd leans in. The songs are loud, rhythmic, and built to stir you up. In Punjabi, a song like that is called a var. Now imagine taking that form, the warrior's ballad, and singing it before sunrise, about God. That's what Guru Nanak did.
screen: `DHADIS WITH DRUM AND SARANGI.` → `BALLADS OF BATTLES AND HEROES.` → `A VAR, ABOUT GOD.`

segments.voice: Var is today's word. In Punjabi poetry, a var is a heroic ballad, a song of praise for a warrior and his deeds, built from stanzas called pauris. Pauri means a step, or a rung of a ladder, and the ballad climbs from one to the next. The Guru Granth Sahib holds a number of vars. This one is Guru Nanak's var in raag Asa: twenty-four pauris, each joined to saloks, short couplet-poems, by Guru Nanak and by the second Guru, Guru Angad. So where's the hero? In Asa di Var, the hero is God: the One who made Himself and the world, and the true Guru who turns people toward that One. And the battle isn't on a field. It's inside: against pride, against empty ritual, against pretending. Guru Nanak's saloks in this var are sharp. He takes on hypocrisy, caste pride, and religion done for show, and then turns, tenderly, to praise and wonder. It's both a ballad and a reckoning. Asa di Var is sung in gurdwaras in the early morning, in many places before sunrise. Ragis, the trained musicians, usually sing it together with the chhants of Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, weaving his verses in among the pauris. At the Darbar Sahib in Amritsar it is part of the morning's kirtan. Over the next four weeks, we'll walk it pauri by pauri, one rung at a time.
screen: `VAR: A HEROIC BALLAD.` · `PAURI: A STEP, A RUNG.` · `THE HERO IS GOD; THE BATTLE IS WITHIN.` · `SUNG AT DAWN, WITH CHHANTS.` · then, large: `THE DAWN BALLAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to the opening. If you can, find a recording of Asa di Var later and play just its first few minutes. For now, sit tall, the way you'd stand to hear a ballad. Breathe in slowly and imagine the gray light before dawn, a gurdwara hall, the harmonium beginning, voices rising together. Let your attention climb, one breath at a time, like rungs on a ladder. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru with each breath. The bell holds the time.
Var. A Punjabi heroic ballad built of pauris, steps; Guru Nanak's var in raag Asa sings of God as hero, and is sung at dawn.
Your line: the dawn ballad. Tomorrow morning, before you look at your phone, give the first minute of the day to something you'd sing to. Day five hundred thirty-six.

537.title: To the tune of a king's ballad
537.hook: the heading says it's sung to the tune of a folk ballad about a king, and ragis sing it with chhants between
537.howItsDone: The heading of Asa di Var names the folk tune of Tunda Asraj, and ragis sing it each morning interwoven with the chhants of Guru Ram Das.

segments.voice: Yesterday, var, and your line: the dawn ballad. Did the first minute of your morning go to something worth singing to? Today, before a single pauri, we read the small print at the top of Asa di Var. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

Plenty of hymns borrowed their tunes from somewhere else. A melody from a tavern, a folk song everybody's grandmother knew, a march from a parade ground: give it new words and suddenly a whole room can sing along, because they already know how it goes. The trick is old, and it's everywhere. Above the first line of Asa di Var in the Guru Granth Sahib, there's a heading. It's easy to skip right past it. It names the old tune to use.
screen: `A HYMN ON A BORROWED TUNE.` → `EVERYONE ALREADY KNOWS HOW IT GOES.` → `THE HEADING ABOVE ASA DI VAR.`

segments.voice: The heading says, in paraphrase: Asa, the first Guru. A var, with saloks, and saloks also written by the first Guru, to be sung to the tune of Tunda Asraj. Dhunee is the word for tune. And Tunda Asraj was the subject of a folk ballad people in Punjab knew: Asraj, a king, often described as tunda, maimed or one-handed. The story behind the ballad is told in more than one version, usually about a prince who's wronged and wounded but rises to rule. The Guru Granth Sahib doesn't retell it. It just names the tune, and expects the singer to know how it goes. That's the striking thing. The heading doesn't point to a sacred melody that only the trained could sing. It points to a folk tune ordinary people already carried in their heads, and the var gives it new words: words about God as the true King, and about the inner battle. Some other vars in the Guru Granth Sahib carry similar headings, naming the folk tunes they were meant to follow. Then there's how it's sung today. Ragis usually pair Asa di Var with the chhants of Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, also in raag Asa. A chhant is sung, then a pauri with its saloks, then the next chhant, so the fourth Guru's verses and the first Guru's ballad take turns. Three Gurus' voices, braided together, at dawn. Old tunes, new words, and many hands in the weaving.
screen: `THE HEADING: TUNDA ASRAJ'S TUNE.` · `DHUNEE: A TUNE PEOPLE KNEW.` · `A FOLK TUNE, NEW WORDS.` · `CHHANTS AND PAURIS TAKE TURNS.` · then, large: `OLD TUNES, NEW WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hum any old tune. Pick a melody you've known for years: a lullaby, a song from childhood, something your family sang in the car. Hum it softly, slowly. Notice how your body already knows it, how the next note arrives before you think. Then let the humming fade, and sit with the quiet it leaves. If you pray, you can let Waheguru ride on the tune as you hum. The bell holds the time.
Dhunee, tune or melody: Asa di Var's heading names the dhunee of Tunda Asraj, an old melody, given new words about God.
Your line: old tunes, new words. Today, take one old habit, a walk, a commute, a chore, and give it a new purpose, like a borrowed tune. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

538.title: A hundred times a day
538.hook: balihaaree gur aapne: I'm a sacrifice to my Guru a hundred times a day, who made angels of men (Asa di Var, ang 462)
538.howItsDone: Asa di Var opens with Guru Nanak's salok of gratitude to the Guru, balihaaree, a hundred times a day, sung in gurdwaras each morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dhunee, and your line: old tunes, new words. Did an old habit get a new purpose? Today Asa di Var opens its mouth, and its very first words are thanks. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

Ask people about a teacher who changed their life and watch their faces. A high school English teacher who said, you can write. A coach who saw something before anyone else did. A grandmother who taught them to pray, or to cook, or to forgive. Plenty of those teachers never heard a real thank-you, or heard it once, years too late. Guru Nanak opens his great ballad not with God's power, not with a warning, but with a thank-you to the Guru, said a hundred times a day.
screen: `A TEACHER WHO CHANGED A LIFE.` → `WE RARELY SAY THANK YOU.` → `A HUNDRED TIMES A DAY.`

segments.voice: The first salok of Asa di Var, in paraphrase: I am a sacrifice to my Guru a hundred times a day, who made angels out of human beings, and took no time to do it. Balihaaree is the first word. It means I am a sacrifice to you, I'd give myself for you. It's the language of overflowing love and gratitude, the kind a mother might whisper over a child. Diuhaarree sad vaar: in a day, a hundred times. Not once, at a graduation. Over and over, every day. Then the reason. Maanas te devte: from humans, devtas, angels or godlike beings. The Guru's teaching takes ordinary, struggling people and makes them shine. And karat na laagee vaar: in the doing of it, there was no delay. Listen to that last word, vaar. Here it means delay. Just before, sad vaar meant a hundred times. And the whole bani is a var, a ballad. Some listeners hear a play on that sound in the very first salok. Who is the Guru here? For Guru Nanak, the true Guru is ultimately God, the Word that teaches from within; Sikhs also honor the human Gurus who carried that Word, and today the Guru Granth Sahib itself. The salok doesn't separate them. It just overflows with thanks. And there's an idea folded in. The salok doesn't picture people climbing to the angels by sheer effort. It pictures a teacher who lifts. The first emotion of Asa di Var, before any argument, is gratitude for being lifted.
screen: `BALIHAAREE: I'D GIVE MYSELF FOR YOU.` · `A HUNDRED TIMES, EVERY DAY.` · `FROM HUMANS, ANGELS, WITHOUT DELAY.` · `GRATITUDE BEFORE ANY ARGUMENT.` · then, large: `MADE ANGELS OF MEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank your teacher. Sit and let one teacher come to mind: a schoolteacher, a parent, a mentor, an author, someone who lifted you. Picture their face. Remember one specific thing they gave you. Then, silently, thank them, as fully as you can. If it rises, thank them again, and again. If you pray, you can also thank the Guru, or God, as the teacher behind all teachers, and say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Balihaaree, I am a sacrifice to you: Asa di Var's first salok says balihaaree to the Guru a hundred times a day, who made angels of humans without delay.
Your line: made angels of men. Today, send one real thank-you message to a teacher who lifted you, even if it's years late. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

539.title: A hundred moons
539.hook: if a hundred moons rose and a thousand suns, without the Guru it would still be dark (Asa di Var M2, ang 463)
539.howItsDone: Asa di Var's second salok, by Guru Angad, is sung each morning in gurdwaras: a hundred moons and a thousand suns would still leave darkness without the Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, balihaaree, and your line: made angels of men. Did a late thank-you go out? A week ends today: peace in remembering, Sukhmani whole, Sukhmani kept; then var, the dawn ballad, its borrowed tune, and its first thanks. Now, the second Guru speaks. Day five hundred thirty-nine.

A stadium at night, every floodlight on. Every seat, every sign, every blade of grass lit up. And in the middle of all that light, someone sits who still doesn't know where they're going, or why. They can read every word on the scoreboard, and none of it tells them which way to turn. A life can look like that: full of light, information, options, screens, and inside, somehow still dark. Guru Angad has a salok for exactly that.
screen: `A STADIUM, EVERY LIGHT ON.` → `SOMEONE IN THE MIDDLE, STILL LOST.` → `A HUNDRED MOONS.`

segments.voice: Right after Guru Nanak's opening salok of thanks comes a second salok, by Guru Angad, the second Guru. In paraphrase: if a hundred moons were to rise, and a thousand suns came up, even with all that light, without the Guru there would be pitch darkness. Chand is moon. Sooraj is sun. Chaanan is light, the ordinary Punjabi word for brightness, daylight, a lamp's glow. And ghor andhaar is deep, pitch-black darkness. Notice the size of the picture. One moon is enough to walk home by. One sun is enough for a whole world. Guru Angad multiplies them, a hundred and a thousand, as if to say: pile up all the outer light you like. It doesn't reach the place he means. That place is inside. The light that tells you who you are, what matters, which way to turn. In Sikh teaching that light comes through the Guru: the Word that teaches from within, carried by the Gurus and now by the Guru Granth Sahib. Without it, a person can be surrounded by brightness and still be stumbling. Set it beside yesterday's salok. Guru Nanak gave thanks for a Guru who turns humans into angels. Guru Angad explains why the thanks runs so deep: everything else, however bright, still leaves us in the dark. This is the voice of a student, too. Guru Angad was Guru Nanak's disciple before he became Guru. Here, in his own salok, he says what his teacher meant to him.
screen: `GURU ANGAD'S SALOK.` · `A HUNDRED MOONS, A THOUSAND SUNS.` · `GHOR ANDHAAR: STILL PITCH DARK.` · `THE LIGHT THAT IS INSIDE.` · then, large: `THE GURU IS THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in the dark a moment. If you can, turn off the lights or close the curtains, or simply close your eyes and cup your hands over them. Let the darkness be complete. Sit in it without hurrying. Notice that even here, something in you is awake: the breath, the knowing that you're here. Rest in that inner light, quiet and small. If you pray, you can say Waheguru into the dark. The bell holds the time.
Chaanan, light or brightness: Guru Angad's salok asks what a hundred moons and a thousand suns, all that chaanan, can do, leaving pitch darkness without the Guru, the light within.
Your line: the guru is the light. Tonight, before you turn off the last light, sit for a breath in the dark and notice what's still lit inside. Day five hundred thirty-nine.
